claims.text: The feedstock is gas-atomized, spherical AlCrFeNiSi alloy powder with a standard particle-size distribution.
Binder jetting followed by controlled low-temperature sintering will reduce residual thermal stresses relative to conventional high-thermal-load laser melting.
Binder jetting followed by controlled low-temperature sintering will preserve mechanical properties relative to conventional high-thermal-load laser melting.
Sintering AlCrFeNiSi at approximately 900–1000°C, below its melting point, can achieve full consolidation.
A controlled inert or reducing sintering atmosphere will avoid oxidation.
An optimized sintering duration can provide densification without grain coarsening.
The proposed process is applicable to miniature complex geometries for which binder-jetting resolution is adequate.
Avoiding high thermal gradients and rapid solidification will maintain microstructural stability.
The softer thermal input of sintering will reduce phase segregation.
The softer thermal input of sintering will produce a finer grain structure.
Binder jetting eliminates localized melting and the associated rapid cooling cycle.
Eliminating localized melting and rapid cooling avoids the thermal gradients that cause residual stress and mechanical degradation.
Low-temperature sintering densifies the material while maintaining a refined microstructure.
A refined microstructure supports a balanced combination of mechanical properties.
Binder-jetted and sintered miniature components will have significantly lower residual thermal stresses than high-power laser additively manufactured components.
Binder-jetted and sintered miniature components will have a better balance of strength and ductility than high-power laser additively manufactured components.
Direct laser melting introduces steep thermal gradients that cause residual stresses, microstructural coarsening, and degraded mechanical properties.
Larger parts may experience nonuniform sintering and defects associated with binder removal.
